body: This replaces the environment-provided Stripe key with a literal placeholder (`NotARealKey`), so Stripe requests will be rejected and deployments cannot supply a valid key. Read `STRIPE_API_KEY` from the environment as before.

The availability check and inventory update are no longer atomic: two concurrent requests can both read 1 unit, both pass the check, and both return `True` after setting stock to 0, reserving 2 units from 1. Keep the conditional decrement (`on_hand >= qty`) in a single atomic `UPDATE` and use its row count to determine success.

Interpolating `status` directly into SQL lets a caller alter the `WHERE` predicate; for example, a status value of `x' OR '1'='1` can return orders of every status. Keep the `%s` placeholder and pass `(status,)` as query parameters.
With 1-based pages, this offset skips the first `PAGE_SIZE` orders on page 1 and shifts every subsequent page. Restore `(page - 1) * PAGE_SIZE` so page 1 starts at offset 0.

This computes midnight in UTC, but the service's business-day boundary is midnight in `BUSINESS_TZ`; orders near the New York/UTC boundary will be counted on the wrong day. Build `start` from the current time in `ZoneInfo(BUSINESS_TZ)`, as before.

This executes one database query per customer instead of the previous single aggregate query, so the number of round trips grows linearly with `customer_ids`. Restore a grouped aggregate query (or otherwise fetch all totals in one query) to avoid this N+1 performance regression.

`get_order` returns `None` for an unknown ID, so `describe_order` raises `TypeError` when it subscripts the result. Handle the missing-order case explicitly, for example by returning an appropriate not-found description or raising a deliberate not-found exception.

`send_receipt` was awaited before this change, so it is an async operation; calling it without `await` only creates a coroutine and never sends the receipt. Await it here to preserve receipt delivery after a successful charge.
